question: Will the UK increase the qualifying period for settlement to 10 years before May 2026?
summary: There is credible momentum toward a 10-year baseline for settlement with an earned-settlement mechanism, supported by official White Paper material and public consultations.
Objections identify real risks—legislative timing, route-specific carve-outs, and transitional rules—that could delay universal adoption to May 2026.

forecasts.reference-class: UK immigration policy reform on settlement (ILR) waiting periods, specifically a baseline 10-year qualifying period with an earned-settlement mechanism to shorten for certain migrants

sources.claim: The default baseline qualifying period for settlement would be increased to 10 years, with reductions possible under an earned-settlement framework based on integration, contribution, residence, and character.
The government announced a baseline 10-year settlement path with a public consultation through February 2026, with potential exceptions and variations by category.
White Paper (May 2025) proposed extending the baseline to 10 years and introducing earned settlement to shorten the period for certain migrants.
The Guardian reports that the government proposed extending the waiting period for permanent settlement to 10 years as part of immigration reform.

The government announced on 20 November 2025 details of a proposal to set a 10-year baseline qualifying period for settlement, with exceptions, and indicated possible implementation from April 2026 if adopted (subject to a public consultation through February 2026).

The Migration Observatory describes a shift to a 10-year baseline for settlement with important exceptions, and notes that a public consultation is open through February 2026; many migrants would face longer waiting periods under the proposed framework.
The June 2025 Immigration Rules publication sets out how qualifying periods are calculated and confirms that periods are route-specific, signaling ongoing reform of settlement rules.
The long residence route currently requires 10 years of continuous lawful presence to qualify for settlement.
KPMG highlights a proposed 'Earned Settlement' framework with a 10-year standard baseline for most migrants, and potential faster paths for certain high-contribution groups.
The government announced it would double the permanent settlement qualifying period for migrants to 10 years, with reductions for those making a strong contribution to British life.
The consultation states the default qualifying period for settlement will be 10 years, with options to set different lengths (5, 10, 15, or 20) depending on contributions; baseline is 10 years.
House of Commons Library notes that the government has proposed a 10-year baseline for settlement, with variations by route, and examples of shorter/longer pathways.
The Guardian reports that the white paper proposals would extend the waiting period for permanent settlement for many migrants to 10 years, indicating broad policy direction in 2025.

synthesis: The ensemble signals a high likelihood of a 10-year baseline by May 2026, but substantive objections regarding legislative timing and route carve-outs introduce meaningful uncertainty. Calibrating downward from the ensemble to reflect these risks yields a final probability around 0.75 with a plausible range of 0.65–0.85.
